Patient Information

Neck Pain: Ergonomics and Gentle Strengthening

How to set up your desk, phone, car and pillow — and a short daily programme of gentle neck and shoulder-blade exercises that has good evidence behind it.

Your head weighs about five kilograms and sits on top of a narrow, mobile column of seven small joints, held up by muscles that are working every minute you are awake. Neck pain is common for the same reason shoulder ache is common in someone carrying a bag all day: not because anything is broken, but because a modest load applied for a long time is hard work.

That is the good news. It means the two levers that matter are how the load is arranged — your desk, your phone, your car, your pillow — and how much endurance the supporting muscles have. Both are things you can change, and neither requires a gym.

An honest word about posture

You have probably been told that bad posture causes neck pain. The evidence for that is weaker than the confidence with which it is asserted: studies find only a modest and inconsistent relationship between how people hold their heads and whether their necks hurt. What matters more is how long you stay in one position and how much muscular endurance you have. So the advice here is not 'sit up straight' — it is 'move often, and build endurance'.

How to use this sheet
  • Read it once through, then start with the first two or three exercises only.
  • Add an exercise every week or two rather than starting everything at once.
  • Print it, tick off the days, and bring it back to your appointment.
  • This sheet is general information for my patients. If you have been given different, specific advice about your own condition, that advice comes first.

Why necks ache

Four contributors, in roughly the order they matter.

⏳ Duration, not position

Any position becomes uncomfortable if you hold it for three hours. Static muscle work restricts its own blood supply, and the ache that follows is the result. Breaking the time up matters more than perfecting the position.

🪫 Poor endurance in the deep muscles

Small deep muscles at the front of the neck are meant to hold the head steady all day. When they fatigue, the big surface muscles take over — and they are sprinters, not marathon runners. They tire, tighten and ache.

👀 Your eyes drag your head forwards

Screens that are too low, too far away, or too small pull the head forwards without you noticing. A great deal of 'neck strain' is really a vision problem — including out-of-date glasses and the reading segment of multifocals.

😬 Stress and jaw clenching

Neck and jaw muscles are among the first to tighten under stress, and clenching at night is very common. If your neck pain tracks your stress levels, treat the stress as part of the neck treatment — my stress management page covers the techniques.

Setting up the workstation

Spend twenty minutes doing this properly once. It outperforms almost anything else on this page.

WhatWhere it should beWhy
Screen heightTop of the screen at or a little below eye levelSo you look slightly down with your eyes, not with your neck
Screen distanceAbout an arm's length away — further for a big screenToo close makes you crane; too far makes you lean in
Text sizeBig enough to read without leaning forwardThe cheapest ergonomic fix there is
Chair heightFeet flat on the floor, knees roughly level with hipsA footrest if your feet dangle
Back supportBottom right back in the chair, low back supportedA rolled towel works as well as a lumbar cushion
ElbowsClose to your sides, bent about 90°, forearms levelReaching forward for the keyboard loads the neck and shoulders
Keyboard and mouseDirectly in front, on the same level, mouse close inA mouse out to the side is a common cause of one-sided neck ache
LaptopsOn a riser or a stack of books, with a separate keyboard and mouseA laptop cannot have both the screen and the keyboard in the right place at once
DocumentsOn a stand beside the screen, at the same heightReading from the desk means hours of looking down
PhoneHeadset or speaker if you are on it a lotCradling a handset on your shoulder is the single worst neck position

Sit-stand desks are useful mainly because they make you change position — the benefit comes from the changing, not from the standing. If you have one, alternate every 30 to 60 minutes rather than standing all day.

The rule that beats all of the above

Get up every 30 to 45 minutes. No workstation setup survives three unbroken hours. Set a timer, or hook it to something natural — the end of each meeting, each phone call, each chapter. And every 20 minutes, look at something at least six metres away for 20 seconds; it rests the eye muscles that are quietly pulling your head forwards.

The daily programme

About ten minutes. Expect the first improvement at four to six weeks, and the real gains by three months.

Range of movement — the morning loosener

5 slow repetitions each direction, morning and evening
Gentle mobility

Neck pain makes people hold still, and holding still makes the neck stiffer and more painful. This breaks the cycle.

  1. Sit tall. Move slowly and smoothly, never forcing.
  2. Turn your head to look over your right shoulder, then your left. Five each way.
  3. Tilt your right ear towards your right shoulder, then the left. Five each way.
  4. Nod your chin down towards your chest, then lift it to look slightly up — only slightly. Five each way.
  5. Finish by rolling your shoulders backwards five times.
Make it harderTake the movement a little further each week as comfort allows.
Make it easierDo half the range, or do it lying down where the muscles do not have to hold your head up.
SafetyAvoid full circles that roll the head right back into extension, and avoid holding an extreme position with the head back and turned. If a movement causes dizziness, visual disturbance, or pins and needles, stop and tell me.
Why it worksEarly, gentle movement produces better outcomes than rest and collars after neck injury, including after whiplash.

Chin nod (deep neck flexor training)

10-second holds × 10, 1–2 times a day
Best-supported neck exercise

Wakes up the small, deep muscles at the front of the neck that hold your head up all day. When these fail, the big surface muscles take over, tire, and ache.

  1. Lie on your back with your knees bent and your head flat on the bed or floor. Use a folded towel under your head only if lying flat forces your chin up.
  2. Without lifting your head at all, make a slow, gentle nodding movement — as if saying a small 'yes', or gently lengthening the back of your neck.
  3. The movement is tiny. Almost nothing should be visible from the outside.
  4. Feel the front of your throat: the big muscles running down the sides of your neck should stay soft. If they tighten and stand out like cords, you are pushing far too hard.
  5. Hold the nod for 10 seconds, breathing normally, then fully relax for 10 seconds.
  6. Repeat 10 times. Stop the set early if you can no longer keep the surface muscles relaxed.
Make it harderOnce you can do 10 × 10 seconds cleanly lying down, hold the nod and lift your head one centimetre off the bed for 5 seconds. Then progress to doing the nod sitting upright against a wall, which is how you will use it in real life. A physiotherapist can grade this more precisely using a pressure cuff, which is worth doing if you are not making progress.
Make it easierShorten the hold to 3–5 seconds and do more repetitions. Effort matters less than doing it without the surface muscles.
SafetyThis should never be forceful and should not hurt. Jamming the chin hard into your chest is the commonest error and will make you sore.
Why it worksThis is the home version of the craniocervical flexion training developed by Jull and colleagues in Queensland. In the clinic it is done with a small pressure cuff behind the neck, working through five graded levels with 10-second holds, and it is deliberately low-load: the aim is to recruit the deep muscles without the surface muscles joining in. Training them this way restores the normal pattern of muscle activation and reduces neck pain — something that strength training alone does not achieve.

Gentle neck isometrics (four directions)

5-second holds × 5 in each direction, once daily
Static strengthening

Builds neck strength without moving the joints at all — which is why it suits a neck that hurts when it moves.

  1. Sit tall in a chair, shoulders relaxed, looking straight ahead.
  2. Forwards: place your palm on your forehead. Press your head gently into your hand and your hand back into your head, so nothing moves. Use about a third of your strength. Hold 5 seconds, then relax.
  3. Backwards: lace your fingers behind your head and press your head back into your hands, again without moving.
  4. Sideways: put your palm against the side of your head above the ear, and press your head into it. Repeat on the other side.
  5. Do five holds in each direction, resting a few seconds between each.
  6. Breathe out during each hold — do not hold your breath.
Make it harderIncrease to 10-second holds, then to about half your maximum effort. Add a rotation direction: place your palm on your cheekbone and resist turning.
Make it easierUse a very light effort — 10% — and 3-second holds. Even that is enough to start.
SafetyNever push to your maximum, and never hold your breath. If a direction reproduces arm pain, pins and needles, or dizziness, stop that direction and tell me.
Why it worksIn a randomised trial of 180 women with chronic neck pain published in JAMA in 2003, both isometric strength training and endurance training over 12 months reduced pain and disability substantially, while stretching and general aerobic exercise alone were much less effective. Most of the gain came in the first two months, and it continued to build over the year.

Shoulder blade squeezes

10 × 5-second holds, 2–3 times a day
Postural endurance

The muscles between your shoulder blades hold your upper back upright. When they give up, your head drifts forwards and the neck carries the load.

  1. Sit or stand tall, arms hanging by your sides, shoulders down.
  2. Draw your shoulder blades gently back and down — as if sliding them into your back pockets. Not up towards your ears.
  3. It is a small movement. Hold for 5 seconds while breathing normally.
  4. Relax completely, then repeat 10 times.
  5. Do a set every time you get up from your desk.
Make it harderHold for 10 seconds. Then do it with your arms out at shoulder height, or holding a light resistance band and pulling it apart.
Make it easierDo it lying on your back, where gravity helps.
SafetyKeep your neck long and your jaw relaxed. If you feel it in your upper trapezius (the ridge between neck and shoulder), you are shrugging.
Why it worksScapular and shoulder-girdle strengthening is part of most successful neck-pain exercise programmes; treating the neck without the shoulder girdle is treating half the problem.

Wall angels

10 slow repetitions, 1–2 times a day
Mobility + posture

Opens the front of the chest and restores the upper-back extension that a day at a keyboard takes away.

  1. Stand with your back against a wall, feet about 20 cm out from it, knees slightly bent.
  2. Flatten your low back gently towards the wall, and rest the back of your head against it — if your head does not reach, stand with a folded towel behind it rather than forcing it back.
  3. Put your arms against the wall in a 'goalpost' position, elbows bent to 90° at shoulder height, backs of hands touching the wall.
  4. Slowly slide your arms up the wall as far as you can while keeping hands, elbows and head in contact, then slide back down.
  5. Move slowly and stop where contact is lost — that point is your current limit, and it will improve.
Make it harderSlide higher; hold for 3 seconds at the top; do it with your feet closer to the wall.
Make it easierDo it seated in a firm chair, or lying on the floor with the arms sliding on the carpet.
SafetyDo not force your head back against the wall or arch your low back to get further.
Why it worksChest and thoracic mobility work is a standard adjunct in neck programmes; a stiff upper back forces the neck to compensate.

Upper trapezius and levator stretches

30 seconds × 3 each side, as often as helpful
Symptom relief

Eases the tight band between neck and shoulder that aches by mid-afternoon. Relief is temporary — this is for comfort, while the strengthening does the lasting work.

  1. Sit tall on a chair and hold the seat with your right hand to anchor that shoulder down.
  2. For the trapezius: tilt your left ear towards your left shoulder. Rest your left hand lightly over your head to add a little weight — do not pull hard.
  3. Hold for 30 seconds of comfortable stretch, never pain. Repeat three times, then swap sides.
  4. For the levator scapulae: from the same anchored position, turn your nose towards your left armpit and gently lower your chin, so the stretch is felt at the back corner of the neck.
  5. Hold 30 seconds, three times each side.
Make it harderNone needed — this is not a strengthening exercise.
Make it easierUse no hand on the head at all; the weight of your head is enough.
SafetyStretch, not pull. Stop if you get pins and needles down the arm, or dizziness.
Why it worksStretching gives short-term relief; the durable improvements in chronic neck pain come from the strengthening and endurance work, which is why the stretches sit alongside them rather than replacing them.

The two-minute desk reset

Every 30–45 minutes
Do this hourly

No posture is a good posture if you hold it for three hours. The dose of a position matters more than the position itself.

  1. Stand up. That alone is most of the benefit.
  2. Do ten shoulder-blade squeezes.
  3. Do five slow neck turns each way.
  4. Look at something at least six metres away for twenty seconds — this rests the eye muscles, and eye strain drives head-forward posture.
  5. Sit back down deliberately, with your bottom right to the back of the chair.
Make it harderSet a timer, or attach it to a natural trigger such as the end of each meeting or each phone call.
Make it easierEven standing and taking three breaths is worth doing.
SafetyNone.
Why it worksFrequent short breaks reduce discomfort in office workers and are one of the few ergonomic measures with reasonably consistent trial support — more consistent than any particular chair or desk.

WhenWhatTime

The rest of the day

Your phone

Bring the phone up towards your face rather than dropping your head towards the phone. Rest your elbows on a table, a cushion or your other hand, so your arms are not holding the weight.

Be sceptical of the 'text neck' headlines: looking down does increase the load on the neck, but the claim that phones are causing an epidemic of neck damage runs well ahead of the evidence. Duration is again the real issue — a long session in any position is the problem, not the position itself.

Your pillow

There is no single best pillow, and expensive ones have not been shown to outperform cheap ones. What matters is that your head is supported in line with your body: on your side, the pillow must fill the gap between your ear and the mattress; on your back, it should support the hollow of your neck without pushing your head forwards.

Do not sleep on your front. It requires you to turn your head to one end of its range for hours at a time, and it is the commonest cause of waking with a locked, painful neck.

A rolled towel inside the pillowcase, positioned under the neck, is a cheap and often very effective experiment before you buy anything.

Driving

Sit tall with the seat upright enough that your shoulders touch the backrest. Set the head restraint so its middle is level with the top of your ears and as close to the back of your head as is comfortable — this is a genuine protection against whiplash in a rear-end collision, not a headrest for comfort.

On long drives, stop every couple of hours and do the two-minute desk reset.

Carrying things

A heavy bag on one shoulder for years is a real and reversible cause of one-sided neck ache. Use a backpack with both straps, or swap sides deliberately and often, or use a wheeled case.

Heat, and what to do in a flare

Heat for 15 to 20 minutes helps most people with muscular neck pain, and is worth doing before the exercises rather than instead of them. Ice suits some people better after an acute strain — use whichever works for you.

Keep moving the neck gently through a flare. Rest and collars prolong recovery; that has been shown repeatedly, including after whiplash injuries.

Questions people ask me

"Should I wear a soft collar?"

Almost never. Collars weaken the muscles you need and slow recovery, including after whiplash, where early gentle movement produces better outcomes than immobilisation. There are specific exceptions after fractures or surgery, which will be explained to you at the time.

"Is it safe to crack my own neck?"

The habit of forcefully twisting your own neck to make it click is worth breaking: it gives brief relief through joint receptors, does nothing lasting, and tends to become compulsive. I would also avoid vigorous high-velocity manipulation of the neck by others — the risk of arterial injury is very small but it is not zero, and gentler treatments work about as well.

"My scan shows degenerative changes and disc bulges."

So does almost everyone's after middle age, including people with no pain whatsoever. These findings correlate poorly with symptoms. They matter when they line up with a specific pattern of arm pain, weakness or numbness — which is precisely what your examination is for.

"The pain goes down my arm with pins and needles."

That suggests irritation of a nerve root, which behaves differently from muscular neck pain. Most cases improve over weeks to a few months. Tell me about it — particularly if there is weakness, if the arm pain is worse than the neck pain, or if it is not settling — and be cautious with end-range neck movements in the meantime.

"How hard should I push these exercises?"

Gently. The chin nod is nearly invisible from the outside, and the isometrics use a third of your strength. Neck exercises that hurt more afterwards were done too hard. Progress by adding time and repetitions before adding effort.

"How long until this helps?"

Four to six weeks for the first clear change, and around three months for the substantial gains — that is the timeframe in the trials of neck strengthening, some of which followed people for a year with benefits sustained. The exercises need to become a permanent, small part of your week rather than a course you finish.

Hurt is not the same as harm

Muscles that have worked will ache. As a rule of thumb, discomfort up to about 4 or 5 out of 10 during and after exercise is acceptable, provided it settles back to your normal level within 24 hours and is not getting worse week on week. Sharp, sudden or one-sided pain is a reason to stop.

Making it actually happen

The best programme is the one you will still be doing in three months. These are the things that reliably make the difference.

🔗 Attach it to something you already do

Balance work while the kettle boils. Neck exercises after brushing your teeth. Relaxation practice as you get into bed. A new habit hooked onto an old one survives; a new habit floating free does not.

📅 Keep a tick sheet

A calendar on the fridge with a tick for each day. Self-monitoring is one of the few adherence strategies with consistent evidence behind it, and it gives us something real to look at in clinic.

🎯 Set a specific, checkable goal

Not 'improve my balance', but 'stand on one leg for 30 seconds each side by the end of March', or 'walk to the shops and back without stopping'. Write it down.

⏱️ Ten minutes beats an hour you never start

Short daily sessions beat one long weekly effort. The programmes below are designed to be done in ten to twenty minutes, most days, in your own kitchen or hallway.

Almost every trial that produced a real result ran for at least eight to twelve weeks. Judge the programme at three months, not at three days.

Getting extra help in Australia

You do not have to do this alone, and supervised programmes work better than unsupervised ones for people at higher risk.

🩺 Your GP can subsidise allied health

Since 1 July 2025, GP Management Plans and Team Care Arrangements have been replaced by the GP Chronic Condition Management Plan. With one in place, you can access up to five Medicare-rebated allied health services per calendar year — shared across all disciplines, so five physiotherapy sessions means none left for anything else (ten services for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients). Referral is now by an ordinary letter rather than a special form. Ask your GP whether you are eligible.

🏃 Physiotherapist or exercise physiologist

A physiotherapist is the right choice for a specific problem — a painful neck, an unsteady gait, vestibular rehabilitation. An accredited exercise physiologist is the right choice for building and supervising a long-term conditioning programme. Both can be seen privately without a referral.

👥 Community falls programmes

NSW Health and many local councils run group strength-and-balance programmes such as Stepping On. Group programmes add the two things a home sheet cannot: supervision and company. Ask your GP or your local council, or search Active and Healthy NSW.

🏠 My Aged Care and NDIS

If you are over 65 and finding daily tasks harder, a My Aged Care assessment can fund home exercise support, home modifications such as rails, and an occupational therapy home-safety visit. Under 65 with a permanent disability, the same supports may be available through the NDIS.

Contact me, or seek urgent care, if you have
  • Weakness, clumsiness or numbness in the hands, difficulty with buttons or handwriting, or unsteadiness in walking — these can indicate pressure on the spinal cord and need prompt assessment.
  • Any change in bladder or bowel control alongside neck symptoms — this needs emergency assessment.
  • Neck pain after significant trauma or a car accident.
  • Neck pain with fever, unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer.
  • A sudden, severe, unfamiliar neck pain or headache, particularly with dizziness, double vision, slurred speech or facial numbness — this needs emergency assessment.
  • Progressive arm weakness, or arm pain that is worsening rather than settling.
  • Neck pain with severe headache and neck stiffness on bending the chin to the chest, with fever or feeling unwell.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis or Down syndrome with new neck pain — the upper neck joints require specific care in both.
